turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in. This is your routine blood pressure and cholesterol visit, right? How've you been?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the blood pressure and the cholesterol, the usual. But um, not great, honestly. I've been kind of a mess about the pills and I almost canceled.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. What's been going on with them?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, I stopped the cholesterol tablet. I read something online and then I couldn't sleep, and I just stopped.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which one was it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. The 20 — no, wait, it was 40 milligrams. I'm sure of that. I took it at night.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did you stop?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't date it. Last winter, or the one before. Sometime after that article. I really don't know.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, we won't make up a month. What did you read that scared you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That statins wreck your muscles and your memory, and if you stop you'll have a heart attack. Is any of that true? Did I set myself up for a heart attack?

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to tell you that you did. Those articles mix a real thing, muscle aches in some people, with a lot of scare language. Stopping a statin does not by itself cause a heart attack.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Why is that stuff everywhere if it's wrong? I don't get how I'm supposed to know what to trust.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's everywhere because scary headlines travel. The useful bit is the muscle-ache risk, and we can talk about that without the rest of it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): But could it still happen? What are the chances? Should I be in the ER? I've been worried sick. I check my pulse in the grocery store.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crushing chest pain, yes, that is the ER. Checking your pulse at the store is the worry talking, not a heart attack. We'll make a plan, and I'm not going to scold you.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Sorry. My sister says I google too much. We were over there and her dog ate a whole stick of butter, which, um, doesn't matter.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. Are you still taking the blood pressure pill?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The lisinopril. But not every day. I take it every other day.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): The prescription is 20 milligrams by mouth once a day, right?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty, yes. I do every other morning. I got scared it would hurt my kidneys if I took it daily. Is that a real thing? My neighbor's kidneys failed and she was on blood pressure medicine.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can affect the kidneys in some people, which is exactly why we do bloodwork, but skipping on your own isn't the safer version. I'm glad you said it out loud.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I take one today? I didn't, because yesterday was my day. And what if my pressure is already fine and I'm overdoing it?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me check before we answer that. 146 over 88. Pulse 74, regular. Lungs are clear, and there's no swelling around the ankles.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 146 bad? Like stroke bad? My dad had a stroke when he was 71, and I turn 64 in June, so I've been doing the math.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): 146 over 88 is high for you, not an emergency. Thinking out loud, it could be the every-other-day lisinopril, it could be you rushing in here anxious, it could be salt. My working impression is it's mainly the missed doses, but I won't lock that in off one reading.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't even add salt. Well, actually, except on corn. Does that count? And is corn bad?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Corn is fine. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No shortness of breath. No dizziness either, which is weird, I thought high pressure would make me dizzy.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any aching in the legs, or swelling you can see?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Swelling, no. My thighs ache, though. Not terrible, like I walked too far. How long, I can't tell you. Maybe since Thanksgiving, or was it Christmas. I don't know.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the ache is while you've been off the statin. I'm not going to blame a pill you aren't taking. Could be you're deconditioned, could be thyroid, could be nothing serious. I will not put a name on it today.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it myopathy? I saw that word. Do I need a muscle biopsy? Please tell me no.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No biopsy. I am not calling it myopathy. Let's see what the tests say before we name it.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): There's one more thing and it's probably dumb. My husband has diabetes and he takes metformin, a thousand milligrams twice a day. I get tired after pasta and I keep looking at his bottle. Would one of his pills help me?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't take his metformin. That medicine is his, not yours, and being tired after pasta does not mean you have diabetes.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't taken any, I just look. Also, way back, the pharmacy mentioned a baby aspirin, but I was never given it and I never took a single one. Was I supposed to?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave aspirin out. You were never started on it, so it isn't part of what you take.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): If I restart the statin tonight, will my thighs get worse? What dose would you even use? I'm really afraid of the 40.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I was going to do is restart atorvastatin at 20 milligrams by mouth at night, half the old dose, starting tonight, and recheck you in a month.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Tonight, even with the thigh ache? I don't even remember if my cholesterol was high last time. And what if my liver can't take it? My mother had liver trouble, cirrhosis or maybe just fatty liver, nobody explained it to me.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on. The ache, no recent cholesterol number in front of me, and a family liver history I didn't have a minute ago. Scratch the restart. I am not starting the statin today.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So I stay off it? Is a month dangerous? What are you actually testing? I have like ten questions.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to throw in a thyroid test for the aches, and I'm dropping that. The plan is a fasting lipid panel and a comprehensive metabolic panel, liver and kidneys, this week. We revisit the statin decision in a month, not before.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting means nothing after midnight, right? Can I drink water? And what if the thigh ache moves and I think it's my chest and I panic?

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Water is fine. No food for about eight hours. Real chest pressure, shortness of breath, or pain going to the arm or jaw, that is the ER. The thigh ache alone, you can call the office.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And the lisinopril, every day or every other day until the labs? I need you to just say it.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every day. 20 milligrams by mouth each morning, including tomorrow, even though you took one yesterday. If you miss a morning, don't double up, just take the next one.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I get dizzy when I go back to daily? Do I stop again? I don't want to fall in the kitchen.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're lightheaded enough that you might fall, skip that dose and call me. Don't slide back to every other day on your own.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the blood test show if I already ruined something by stopping? I keep thinking the damage is done.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): The lipid panel shows where the cholesterol is now. It cannot time-stamp damage, and I won't pretend it can. That's why the decision waits until I see you in a month.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I book that on the way out? And do you want my husband's pill list, or just mine?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just yours. Book a follow-up with me in one month, and get the labs done this week, fasting. The front desk can set both of those up.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. One month. I'll try not to google tonight. Thanks for not yelling at me.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

omissions.text: Patient had not taken any of her husband's metformin; she only considered it/looked at the bottle.
Baby aspirin was discussed historically by the pharmacy, but the patient states she was never given it and never took a single dose; doctor confirmed aspirin is not part of her regimen.

Planned restart of atorvastatin 20 mg nightly starting tonight was explicitly reversed; doctor said 'Scratch the restart. I am not starting the statin today' and to revisit the statin decision in one month, not before.
Pulse was documented as 74 and regular; the regularity is both a vital sign detail and exam finding tied to the pulse measurement.
Doctor considered but then dropped a thyroid test for the aches.
ER precautions also included crushing chest pain/real chest pressure as a trigger for emergency evaluation, not just shortness of breath or pain to arm/jaw.
Doctor advised the thigh ache alone is not an ER reason and patient should call the office for that symptom alone.
